pr_title: util: runtime deprecate `promisify`-ing a function returning a `Promise`
pr_body:
My goal would be for this deprecation to never reach EOL, and stay as runtime deprecated forever. The warning it produces should help folks who run into the linked issue figure out what's happening.

```js
// file.js

const promisified = promisify(async () => {});

promisified();
```

`node --trace-warnings file.js` will show `at file.js:5:1` – so not where the `promisify` call happened, but where the promisified function was called. Hopefully that will give enough info to debug it.

Fixes: https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/49607

pr_comments: I believe it is not a good pattern to rely on the constructor. The problem is also that this does not determine a function returning a Promise `() => Promise.resolve()`. we would probably also need to check for similar constructors, e.g. `GeneratorFunction` or `AsyncGeneratorFunction`, but I think the same issue applies here as well, it is just syntactic sugar.

It's true that we will never catch all the instances where `promisify` is misused, but it's only emitting a warning, I don't think we need to worry too much about false negative – as long as there are no false positive, it should already be helpful.

True, it's just a warning, but you are preventing anyone from using async functions with a node style callback - albeit likely a bad pattern. `async function foo(nodeSyleCallback) {}`. That said, I believe that's not node.js' responsibility to determine. As far as I know node.js is not doing those kind of checks anywhere in the codebase -- nor should it.

I'm not preventing anything, the function will still work as before. The only difference is that if it's passed to `promisify`, a warning will be emitted (which is not going to break anyone).
I agree that would indeed be a bad pattern, and on top of that using `promisify` is itself more a workaround than a great API, so all in all, I think it's fine to make that use-case less convenient.

I disagree, I think this is a matter of principle.

> I'm not preventing anything, the function will still work as before.

ok, let me rephrase, you are nagging everyone using such a function with promisify.

> and on top of that using promisify is itself more a workaround than a great API,

I don't think that's a good justification to introduce this either. 🤷‍♂️ 

what are you going to do if someone files an issue claiming `promisify(AsyncGeneratorFunction)` does not throw?

this does not make it an async function either:

```
function foo() {}
foo.constructor = 'AsyncFunction'
```

but the check would treat it as such.

> this does not make it an async function either:
> 
> ```
> function foo() {}
> foo.constructor = 'AsyncFunction'
> ```
> 
> but the check would treat it as such.

It wouldn't, let me add a test to demonstrate that.

> It wouldn't, let me add a test to demonstrate that.

ah, sorry, didn't re-check the code, I thought it was checking for the constructor name (string) actually. https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/49609#discussion_r1321947497

Regardless, I still think this is a bad idea.

@lukiano to avoid having an unhandled rejection, folks should not use `promisify` but call the function directly and await its result. I understand what you are trying to do, but I think it's taking it one step too far, and it would be a potential breaking change if some folks rely on the current behavior for some reason.

Thinking a bit more about this, I think this naked warning is a bit weird, I've went ahead and open https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/49647 to make this follow the usual deprecation process, because that's more or less what this warning is: a deprecation warning. When/if the other PR lands, I'll update this one.

It certainly makes me think of functions that both provide a callback and return a value. Often the value returned is a way to cancel the action (e.g. timeouts), which is addressed by `AbortSignal` in the promisified version.

Others, like `stream.Writable.write()` provide different meanings to both outputs. In this one in particular, the callback is called when the data is flushed, and the return value signals if it accepts more data. Likely a promisifed version wouldn't use either, but wait for the `drain` event.

Should we deprecate using `promisify` on any function that returns a value, even if it isn't a `Promise`?

All functions return a value – except if it throws. What this deprecation proposal is attempting to do is help folks who "promisify" async functions, because it's likely a mistake and can be hard to debug (and as you said, rejections would not be handled). Calling `promisify` on a function that returns a value that might be useful is maybe a bad pattern (subjective), but it's not as likely to be a mistake, and does not have the problem of unhandled promise rejections.

issue_context.title: Promisify crashing node (or making it hang)
issue_context.body:
### Version

v20.6.1

### Platform

Linux xxx 6.2.0-31-generic #31-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Mon Aug 14 13:42:26 UTC 2023 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

### Subsystem

_No response_

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

Run this code:
```mjs
import {promisify } from "node:util";


const asyncFunction = async () => 5;

await promisify(asyncFunction)();
console.log('This does not show');
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

Every time

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

Anything but a silent crash... if it's not allowed throw an error, if you do accept async functions maybe promisify should be a noop since async functions already return promises...

I'm no node developer

### What do you see instead?

Status code 0, process exits.

### Additional information

This bug breaks packages like this: https://github.com/semantic-release/commit-analyzer/issues/525
comments:
> Status code 0, process exits.

That's really surprising, I'm getting exit code 13, can you double check if you're seeing an exit code 0?

I can, one sec.

Edit: hmm, you are right, this reproduction is code 13, looking into source repo to see if it might be 13 there as well.

The same code crashing in the code I linked above (https://github.com/semantic-release/commit-analyzer/issues/525) exits with code `0`. I'm no node developer so I'm probably a lot out of my depth here... 

I for sure can't catch whatever error is happening (I tried). 

`process.exitCode` is probably the culprit of hte crash being silent, so it is crashing node but not silent by default...

> An async function is indistinguishable from a sync function

`.constructor.name` allows you to, not sure if it's standard though.

I'll look a bit further. I'm not sure the mistakes you point out mean there is no bug, or my reproduction is simply wrong...
